newsitem.title: UK: UK retail sales don't herald inflationary boom - BRC.
newsitem.headline: UK retail sales don't herald inflationary boom - BRC.

text.p: The British Retail Consortium (BRC) said strong retail spending figures did not herald the start of an inflationary consumer boom and it urged Chancellor Kenneth Clarke to keep interest rates on hold.

In a briefing for retailers, BRC chief economic adviser Andrew Sentance said inflation was likely to fall in the coming months due to a weaker trend in food prices, very low factory gate price increases and a stronger exchange rate.
"In the short term, these downward influences are likely to offset any upward pressure on inflation from the impact of consumer demand on profit margins," he said.
BRC director-general James May said strong August retail sales confirmed the strengthening trend in consumer spending.

"We should not forget that this pickup in the retail sector comes after a slowdown in retail growth of just over one percent last year. There are still many negative influences on the consumer, including job insecurity, negative equity and memories of falling house prices in the recession," he said.
The organisation's advice to the Chancellor of the Exchequer was to keep interest rates as low as possible and make modest tax cuts in his November 26 budget.
Sentance said that as long as interest rates remained at curent levels, consumer spending should continue to grow at the present healthy rate, giving a welcome lift to economic growth.
Worries that consumer-led growth would push up wages and overall inflation were premature.
The pickup in consumer spending was only just beginning, whereas in the late 1980s it went on for four years, and the momentum behind it was much weaker than in the late 1980s.
"The recent rate of GDP growth has been sluggish...and unemployment remains high, so there is some slack to be taken up before inflationary pressures emerge," Sentance said.
"The case for a rise in interest rates now is therefore weak," he added.

"However, as we move into 1997, and particularly after the election, some upward adjustment in borrowing costs could be justified to ensure that consumer growth is kept to a sustainable rate and does not become an inflationary threat."
